intro_en:
The southernmost segment of the Israel National Trail is also one of its high points. A route that has it all: a deep canyon, breathtaking lookouts, a view over four countries, mountains and rocks in a variety of colours – and the Red Sea, the bluest there is.

 Shehoret Canyon – Mount Yehoram (55)
character_en: (For those walking from north to south) The route descends from an elevation of about 700 metres to sea level, but because of a fairly steep climb along the way, the cumulative descent is about 900 metres. Some of the descents are a little steep but well arranged.
pois_en: Gishron Lookout, Nahal Gishron, the Knife-Edge Ridge trail, Mount Tzfahot, the Gulf of Eilat.
important_en: Those walking from south to north who start the Israel National Trail in Eilat walk this segment on a long, steep climb. Alternatively, you can take a taxi or a trail angel to Mount Yoash and walk the segment downhill heading south. The next day you can travel back to Mount Yoash and continue walking north.

If you finish Ma'ale Gishron towards the end of the day and are pressed for time, you can shorten the walk by descending a short trail to the jeep track at the foot of Givat Rehavam and walking east to the road.
At the Mount Yehoram campsite there should be a water tank placed by the Israel Nature and Parks Authority (INPA). Before setting out, it is worth confirming this with the INPA's regional ranger.
description_en:
We leave the overnight campsite on Mount Yehoram from the point where the main road crossing the campsite turns south, and advance along a black-marked trail to the meeting with the Israel National Trail. The black trail enters a channel and within a few minutes' walk we reach the junction with the Israel National Trail.
Near the crossing point of Road 12 (Ma'ale Eilat), we also cross the watershed line between Nahal Netafim and Nahal Gishron. Nahal Gishron flows south, and drains on the Egyptian side of the border into Nahal Taba (Wadi Taba), which empties into the Gulf of Eilat near the Taba Hotel.
Nahal Gishron is one of the most beautiful streams in the Eilat Mountains, and a hike through it is a fitting summary and finale to the hike in this region and to the whole of the Israel National Trail.
The channel of Nahal Gishron is cut close to a long fault line known as the "Gishron Fault", around which there are further, smaller associated faults. Along the fault lines we can see rocks from different geological periods lying side by side on the surface. In the rock walls, chiefly of the soft sandstone, the forces of weathering have sculpted a variety of forms.
It was from this direction, the head of Ma'ale Eilat, that the fighters of the Negev Brigade arrived on their way to Eilat in Operation Uvda in March 1949. When the fighters reached the seashore at the head of the gulf, they raised the famous Ink Flag over the Umm Rashrash police station and announced by telegram: "Convey to the Government of Israel: on the Haganah Day of the 11th of Adar, the Negev Palmach Brigade and the Golani Brigade present the Gulf of Eilat to the State of Israel."
Immediately after crossing the road we pass along an ancient transport route – Darb al-Hajj, meaning the Pilgrims' Way. This is a road laid down in the Mamluk period as a route for Muslim pilgrims from Egypt to Mecca.
The Israel National Trail continues south with a blue-marked trail, advancing along a shelf between Mount Yoash on the left (with antennas on its summit) and the channel of Nahal Gishron on the right.
After a trail junction where a black trail crosses the blue trail, the view opens up with a fine vista across the border, to the south and west – expanses of dark-hued mountains that give a small taste of the landscapes of Sinai. On the right we see the deep, impressive canyon of Nahal Gishron, with the border fence visible inside it.
How did it come about that a border fence was laid inside such an impressive canyon? The border lines in the area have changed several times since they were first set in 1906, between British Egypt and Turkish-ruled Palestine. The border line between Israel and Egypt after the War of Independence was also set along this route. When the peace accords between Israel and Egypt were signed in 1979, Israel undertook to withdraw from Sinai (which it had captured in 1967 in the Six-Day War) and return to the "Mandate border" – the same border line set in 1906. But a dispute arose between the two countries over the route of the border, and this was settled by international arbitration, which determined that the border line would cut across the channel of Nahal Gishron twice.
As a result, the hiking trail that previously descended from here into the deep canyon was changed. The border fence itself was built later, following several terror attacks in which terrorists infiltrated from Sinai into the Road 12 area and harmed civilians and soldiers. The fence was built along a difficult route in a complex and costly engineering operation that was completed in 2013, and its construction right along the border line allows hikers to enter Nahal Gishron despite the proximity to the border.
The Israel National Trail turns onto the descent via a bypass prepared in 1989, after the "horseshoe" of the Nahal Gishron canyon passed to the Egyptian side of the border. The trail descends along a tributary of Nahal Gishron, in a narrow, steep channel. Handholds and ladders assist the descent.
The bypass ends at the meeting with the main channel of Nahal Gishron. The trail turns left, and on the right we see a dry waterfall about 20 metres high with a large rock pool beneath it. From here the channel widens, and acacia trees appear beside the trail as it advances down the stream. After a short walk, the dark granite bedrock gives way to sandstone in shades of red.
We pass two junctions – the first with a red-marked trail climbing to Ma'ale Yehoshafat, and the second with a green trail arriving from Nahal Shlomo via Ma'avar Tzafra. If there is time, it is worth popping over to see the very narrow Ma'avar Tzafra – a beautiful slot in the colourful sandstone. A military road crosses the Israel National Trail and Nahal Gishron on its way to the border fence.
Approaching the second point where Nahal Gishron crosses the border to the Egyptian side, the Israel National Trail leaves the stream eastwards and climbs Ma'ale Gishron.
At the end of the strenuous climb, at the top of the ascent, a conical white hill is visible to the east, standing out against a dark ridge. This is Givat Rehavam, rising out of the Rehavam Valley (Bik'at Rehavam). Geological faults on both sides of the valley created this unique landscape picture: contrasting colours of bedrock from geological periods far apart in time are visible to the eye in a single glance.
The trail turns sharply south with red markings, along the ridge above Nahal Gishron. Looking down, we see the stream channel crossing the border fence to the Egyptian side.
After a short walk we reach a paved military road, and a black trail parallel to the road leads right to a lookout from the head of the spur of the Gishron Cliffs (Tzukei Gishron). For those interested, the walk to the lookout along the black trail is one kilometre each way. The lookout is among the most beautiful in the area, overlooking Nahal Gishron and the expanses beyond the Egyptian border.
The Israel National Trail continues with the red marking, turns left and, after a short distance along the edge of the road, reaches one of the most impressive stretches of today's hike. A landscape of huge limestone flatirons rises at a sharp angle above the valley of Nahal Gishron. The trail passes along a narrow passage at the top of the flatirons, and this stretch of walking is known among hikers as "the Knife-Edge Trail" (Shvil HaSakin). From the trail there is a fine view south and east, and to the east the head of the Gulf of Eilat can also be seen.
After descending from the flatirons, we pass through a concentration of limestone boulders – stones shaped like giant potatoes – on the way to Mount Tzfahot.
At the start of the climb to Mount Tzfahot, the Israel National Trail and the red marking join a green-marked trail that climbs the mountain.
Mount Tzfahot is named after the rock visible on its slopes and summit – a grey rock with a fine layered structure. Slate (tzfaha) is a metamorphic rock – a rock that has undergone change. The slate originated in clay rocks that were buried at great depth, and conditions of intense heat and pressure produced a process of metamorphosis (change) in the structure and composition of the rocks. On the slate rocks in the area there are small, shiny black flakes, made of the mineral mica, one of the components of slate.
From the summit of Mount Tzfahot there is a fine view over the head of the Gulf of Eilat, from the city of Aqaba on the Jordanian side, through Eilat, to Coral Island (Pharaoh's Island) near the shore of the gulf on the Egyptian side. To the north we see Mount Amir, Mount Shehoret, Mount Shlomo and Mount Rehavam.
Approaching the finish and the descent to the Gulf of Eilat, it is fitting to read a few lines from the poem written by Haim Gouri the day before the capture of Eilat in Operation Uvda (March 1949):
The granite cliffs crashing down to the sea
We have seen you, Eilat, Eilat!
From lofty Mount Hermon
To the shore of Eilat –
All of you is mine
The last 3 lines are especially fitting for those finishing the Israel National Trail today.
From the top of Mount Tzfahot all that remains is to "glide" down with the trail – to the shoreline by the Eilat Field School.
Here the segment ends, and here the whole Israel National Trail ends.
nearby_en: Almog Beach (Coral Beach) – a nature reserve with an admission fee, opposite the Eilat Field School.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, Trail Marking Coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
